bava_metzia-5a-13-14.note: People gave a shepherd their animals every day in front of witnesses. One day they handed them over without witnesses, and at day's end he denied ever receiving them. Then witnesses testified that he had eaten two of them. Rabbi Zeira said that by Rabbi Ḥiyya's first ruling, an oath is due about the rest. Abaye objected: is this shepherd, now shown to be a robber, to be trusted to swear? Rabbi Zeira answered that he meant the other side swears and collects.
bava_metzia-5a-13-14.why: The Sages are debating whether witnesses who prove part of a claim, like a defendant who admits part, oblige him to swear about the rest; Rabbi Zeira applies Rabbi Ḥiyya's view to this shepherd.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: Applied Rabbi Ḥiyya's ruling to the shepherd's case.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Objected that a proven robber cannot be trusted to take an oath.

terms.meaning: In a money dispute, a court can require a party to swear to his claim before God; swearing falsely is a grave sin, so an oath settles the matter.
Here, the owners of the animals: when the defendant cannot be trusted to swear, the claimant swears instead and collects.

bava_metzia-6a-18-18.note: Two people were arguing over a bathhouse, each saying it was his. One of them consecrated it to the Temple. Rav Ḥananya, Rav Oshaya and all the Rabbis stayed away from it, and Rav Oshaya asked Rabba to put the question to Rav Ḥisda in Kafrei. On the way, in Sura, Rav Hamnuna told Rabba the answer was in a mishna: an animal that may or may not be a firstborn stays with its owner, yet may not be sheared or worked. Whether that settles the bathhouse is argued out in what follows.
bava_metzia-6a-18-18.why: The Gemara is asking whether a person can consecrate a disputed item that he has not seized; this bathhouse case is brought as the answer.

people.name: Rav Oshaya
people.about: Kept away from the bathhouse and asked Rabba to take the question to Rav Ḥisda.

people.name: Rav Ḥananya
people.about: Also kept away from the consecrated bathhouse.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Carried the question; in Sura he heard Rav Hamnuna's answer.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A Sage in Sura who pointed to a mishna about firstborn animals.

terms.meaning: To dedicate property to the Temple; after that, using it for oneself is forbidden.
A firstborn male animal of a kosher species is holy and goes to a priest; a firstborn son is redeemed from a priest.
The early collection of rabbinic law on which the Gemara comments; also a single teaching from it.

bava_metzia-11a-21-21.note: Rabban Gamliel and other Elders were traveling on a ship. Rabban Gamliel declared that a tenth of his produce, to be measured out later, was given to Yehoshua, and the place where it lay was rented to him; and another tenth was given to Akiva ben Yosef to acquire for the poor, its place also rented to him.
bava_metzia-11a-21-21.why: Ulla has said a person's field acquires things for him only when he stands next to it; Rabbi Abba cites this voyage to challenge him, since Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva were on the ship, far from the field.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Gave away his tithes while at sea.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Yehoshua ben Ḥananya, a Levite, who received the first tithe.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Akiva ben Yosef, who received the poor man's tithe on behalf of the poor.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Raised this incident as an objection to Ulla.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: The Sage whose ruling about acquiring through one's field is challenged.

terms.meaning: A tenth of the harvest that must be set aside: the first tithe goes to a Levite, and in certain years another tithe goes to the poor.
A member of the tribe of Levi, entitled to receive the first tithe.
Here, the leading Sages traveling with Rabban Gamliel.

bava_metzia-18a-12-12.note: A bill of divorce was found in Rav Huna's court, stating it was written in Sheviri City on the Rakhis River. Rav Huna said they must worry there might be two towns called Sheviri, so it could belong to someone else. Rav Ḥisda told Rabba to look into it, since Rav Huna would ask him that evening. Rabba went out, examined the question, and found a mishna: any court document that is found must be returned.
bava_metzia-18a-12-12.why: The Gemara argues that even where caravans pass often, a found bill of divorce is held back only if two people of the same name are known to live there; Rabba's ruling in Rav Huna's busy court is its proof.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Head of the court where the bill of divorce was found.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Told Rabba to research the question before Rav Huna asked him.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Found the mishna that settled the case.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end their marriage.
A document produced or confirmed by a court; the mishna says a found one must be returned.

bava_metzia-18b-19-19.note: Rabba bar bar Ḥana lost a bill of divorce he had been given to deliver, in the study hall. When it was found, he said he could give a distinguishing mark for it, and could also recognize it by sight, and it was returned to him. Afterward he said he did not know which had decided it: whether they hold that distinguishing marks count by Torah law, or whether they trusted his recognition only because he is a Torah scholar, which would not be done for an ordinary person.
bava_metzia-18b-19-19.why: Rav Ashi has just said a found bill of divorce is returned only on a clear-cut mark, since it is uncertain whether marks are trusted by Torah law; Rabba bar bar Ḥana's own case leaves that same question open.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Ḥana
people.about: A Sage who lost a bill of divorce he was delivering and got it back.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end their marriage.
A specific feature an owner can describe to prove a found item is his.
Knowing an item by sight without being able to name a specific mark; the Sages trusted this only from Torah scholars.
A rule from the Torah itself, as opposed to one the Sages instituted, which is treated more leniently.

bava_metzia-20a-7-7.note: A bill of divorce found in Rav Huna's court said it was written in Sheviri City on the Rakhis River. Rav Huna worried there might be two towns called Sheviri. Rav Ḥisda sent Rabba to look into it before Rav Huna asked him that evening, and Rabba found the mishna that any court document must be returned. Rav Amram asked how Rabba could settle a ritual matter from a teaching about money. Rabba called him a fool: the mishna also covers documents of ḥalitza and refusal. Then the cedar beam of the study hall gave way, and each of the two said it was because of him.
bava_metzia-20a-7-7.why: The mishna says found court documents must be returned; this incident shows Rabba applying that line to a bill of divorce, and defending the step from money matters to ritual ones.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Head of the court where the bill of divorce was found.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Sent Rabba to research the question.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Found the answer in the mishna and called Rav Amram a fool.

people.name: Rav Amram
people.about: Challenged Rabba's use of a money ruling for a ritual matter.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end their marriage.
The ceremony that releases a childless widow from having to marry her late husband's brother.
A girl married off as a minor could refuse the marriage before coming of age; a document recorded her refusal.
A question of what is permitted or forbidden, such as marriage, as opposed to a question of money.

bava_metzia-22a-9-10.note: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi came to the orchard of Mari bar Isak, and his sharecropper set dates and pomegranates before them. Ameimar and Rav Ashi ate; Mar Zutra did not. Mari bar Isak arrived and asked his sharecropper why he hadn't brought the Sages the better fruit. Ameimar and Rav Ashi asked Mar Zutra why he still would not eat. He answered in Rava's name that such words show an owner's consent only for teruma, a mitzva he is glad to see done; here the owner spoke out of embarrassment.
bava_metzia-22a-9-10.why: The Gemara has just cited a teaching that an owner who says 'you should have taken the better produce' consents to an agent's teruma; the Sages here argue over whether the same words prove consent for ordinary fruit.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: Ate the fruit the sharecropper served.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: Would not eat the fruit, doubting the owner had agreed.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Ate the fruit and questioned Mar Zutra.

people.name: Mari bar Isak
people.about: Owner of the orchard.

terms.meaning: A portion of the harvest given to a priest.
A tenant who farms someone else's land for a share of the crop.
A commandment, or a good deed done in fulfillment of one.

bava_metzia-23b-8-8.note: A man found pitch near a winepress and came to ask Rav what to do with it. Rav told him to take it for himself. Seeing the man still hesitate, Rav said: go and share it with my son Hiyya, showing he was sure it was not stolen property.
bava_metzia-23b-8-8.why: The discussion asks whether the place where an item is found counts as a mark that lets the owner reclaim it. Rav's ruling seems to say no, but Rabbi Abba explains it otherwise: grass had grown through the pitch, so its owner had long given up on it.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Founder of the great academy at Sura in Babylonia, one of the most important early Sages of the Talmud.

people.name: Hiyya
people.about: Rav's son.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: A Sage who explains the reasoning behind Rav's ruling.

terms.meaning: A feature an owner can describe to prove a lost item is his. A finder must announce items that have one; items without one may often be kept.
Once an owner has given up hope of getting a lost item back, it becomes ownerless and the finder may keep it.

bava_metzia-24a-1-1.note: A silver goblet was stolen from the host of Mar Zutra Ḥasida. Mar Zutra saw a student wash his hands and dry them on someone else's cloak, and said this was the one who does not care about other people's property. He bound the student, and the student confessed.

people.name: Mar Zutra Ḥasida
people.about: A Sage whose host's goblet was stolen, and who found the thief.

terms.meaning: An epithet meaning "the pious."

bava_metzia-24b-4-4.note: A man found four dinars tied in a cloth that had been thrown into the Biran River. He came before Rav Yehuda, who told him to go and announce his find. The Gemara explains: things swept off by water usually belong to the finder, but this river has obstacles, so the owner does not give up hope; and though most people there are gentiles, Jews dammed the river and Jews dredge it, so the coins probably fell from a Jew who expects them back.
bava_metzia-24b-4-4.why: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds that things lost to the sea, or where crowds gather, belong to the finder because the owner gives up hope; the Gemara asks whether Rav Yehuda's ruling limits that even where most people are gentiles.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who told the finder to announce the coins.

terms.meaning: A silver coin.
To announce publicly that one has found an item, so its owner can claim it.
The owner's giving up hope of getting a lost item back; once he does, the finder may keep it.

bava_metzia-24b-7-7.note: A kite snatched meat in the marketplace and dropped it among the palm trees of the house of bar Maryon. The man who found it asked Abaye, who told him to take it for himself. The Gemara explains that something carried off by a kite is like something swept away by the sea, which the owner gives up on, and that the meat was not forbidden as unwatched because the finder stood and saw it the whole time.
bava_metzia-24b-7-7.why: The Gemara is testing whether Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's rule, that a finder keeps items lost where the owner gives up hope, holds even where most people are Jews, as in a kosher meat market.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: The Sage who let the finder keep the meat.

terms.meaning: A bird of prey.
Rav's rule that meat left unwatched is forbidden, since no one can be sure where it came from.

bava_metzia-24b-8-8.note: Rabbi Ḥanina found a slaughtered young goat between Tiberias and Tzippori, and the Sages permitted it to him. Rabbi Ami explained: they let him keep it as a found item, following Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, and let him eat it as properly slaughtered, following Rabbi Ḥananya son of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, who permits lost animals that their owner later finds slaughtered.
bava_metzia-24b-8-8.why: The Gemara is asking where Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's rule applies; it goes on to infer from this case that the place had a Jewish majority, and Rava answers that only most of the slaughterers there were Jews.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥanina
people.about: Found the slaughtered goat.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Explained on what grounds the Sages permitted it.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥananya, son of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili
people.about: Permits lost animals found slaughtered.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Forbids lost animals found slaughtered.

terms.meaning: Killed in the ritual way that makes meat kosher; meat from an animal not slaughtered properly is forbidden.
A teaching from the early rabbinic period that was not included in the Mishna.

bava_metzia-24b-10-10.note: Rabbi Ami found slaughtered fledglings between Tiberias and Tzippori. He asked Rabbi Asi (some say Rabbi Yoḥanan, some say the study hall) and was told to take them for himself. Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa found a skein of netting thread and asked Rabbi Yoḥanan (some say the study hall), and was told the same.
bava_metzia-24b-10-10.why: These continue a run of finds that the Sages let the finder keep, in line with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view that owners give up hope of things lost where crowds pass.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Found slaughtered fledglings on the road.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: One of those said to have told Rabbi Ami to keep them.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Asked about both finds, by some accounts.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa
people.about: Found a skein of thread used for nets.

terms.meaning: A loose coil of thread or yarn.

bava_metzia-28b-11-11.note: Rav Pappa's father lost a donkey, and others found it. He came before Rabba bar Rav Huna, who told him to bring witnesses that he was not a swindler. He brought them, and Rabba bar Rav Huna asked: do you know that he is a swindler? They said yes. Rav Pappa's father cried out: I am a swindler? They said they had meant that he was not one. Rabba bar Rav Huna said that was reasonable, since a person does not bring witnesses against himself.
bava_metzia-28b-11-11.why: The Sages ruled that once swindlers multiplied, a claimant must bring witnesses that he is no swindler before taking back a lost item; this incident shows the rule in practice.

people.name: Rav Pappa's father
people.about: Lost a donkey and had to prove he was not a swindler.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: The judge who required witnesses and then accepted them.

terms.meaning: Someone known for false claims; the Sages would not return a lost item to him even if he described its marks.

bava_metzia-30b-5-6.note: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei was walking on the road when he met a man who had set down a load of wood and was resting. The man asked him to lift it onto him. Rabbi Yishmael asked what it was worth, paid him the half-dinar, and declared the wood ownerless. The man took the wood again, and Rabbi Yishmael again paid and declared it ownerless. When he saw the man wanted to take it once more, he said: I made it ownerless for everyone, but not for you.
bava_metzia-30b-5-6.why: Rava has just said a person must help load another's burden only where he would load his own; the Gemara goes on to ask how Rabbi Yishmael could exclude one man, and why he bothered, given that an elderly Sage was exempt.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage asked by a stranger to help lift his load of wood.

terms.meaning: Property declared free for anyone to take.
Half of a silver coin; the price the man named for his wood.

bava_metzia-31b-14-14.note: Issur and Rav Safra were business partners. Rav Safra dissolved the partnership without Issur's knowledge, in front of two witnesses, and came to Rabba bar Rav Huna, who told him to bring the court of three before whom he had divided it, or witnesses to that. Rabba bar Rav Huna cited the mishna that a stipulation is made before a court; Rav Safra answered that taking his own share was only making a fact known, for which two witnesses are enough, just as a widow sells estate property without a court. Abaye countered that even the widow needs a court of laymen. The text does not say how the case ended.
bava_metzia-31b-14-14.why: The mishna has just taught that a finder may make his condition about lost wages before a court; the story argues over whether that line proves a court is needed whenever one claims property tied up with someone else's.

people.name: Issur
people.about: Rav Safra's partner in a joint business venture.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: Issur's partner, who split their property without telling him.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage Rav Safra came to, who demanded a court of three.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Challenges Rav Safra's proof from the widow.

terms.meaning: The core collection of early rabbinic law; the Gemara is the later discussion built around it.
The smallest Jewish court, made up of three judges, needed for many legal acts.
A court of three ordinary people rather than ordained expert judges.

bava_metzia-33a-14-14.note: Rav Hisda asked his teacher Rav Huna what the law is for a student whose teacher needs him. Rav Huna took the question as being about himself and said: Hisda, Hisda, I do not need you; you need me for forty years. The two grew angry and stopped visiting each other. Rav Hisda observed forty fasts because Rav Huna had been offended, and Rav Huna observed forty fasts because he had wrongly suspected Rav Hisda.
bava_metzia-33a-14-14.why: The Gemara is asking which teacher's lost item a person must return before his own father's; Rav Hisda's question extends that to a student who is also his teacher's study partner.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Rav Huna's disciple and study partner, who asked the question.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Rav Ḥisda's teacher, who took offense at the question.

terms.meaning: Days of fasting taken on as an act of regret and atonement.

bava_metzia-35a-7-7.note: A man left jewels with another for safekeeping. When he asked for them back, the keeper said he did not know where he had put them. Rav Nahman ruled that saying I do not know is itself negligence and ordered him to pay. When he did not pay, Rav Nahman had his palace seized to cover the jewels. Later the jewels turned up, and they had risen in value. Rav Nahman ruled that the jewels go back to their owner and the palace goes back to its owner.
bava_metzia-35a-7-7.why: Right after it, Rava asks why the keeper did not keep the jewels, like a bailee who pays instead of swearing, and explains that this keeper had forced the owner into court, so the rule does not apply.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The judge who ordered payment and then reversed the seizure.

terms.meaning: Someone who holds another person's property for safekeeping. Jewish law sets different levels of responsibility for a paid and an unpaid bailee if the item is lost or stolen.
Careless guarding. A bailee who was negligent must pay for what was lost.

bava_metzia-36a-10-11.note: Some gardeners used to leave their spades every day with a certain old woman. One day they left them with one of the gardeners instead. He heard the noise of a wedding, went out to it, and left the spades with the old woman. While he was away, the spades were stolen. Rav exempted him from paying.
bava_metzia-36a-10-11.why: Rav and Rabbi Yohanan dispute whether a bailee who hands a deposit to another bailee is liable. Rav Hisda says Rav's view was only inferred from this ruling, wrongly: here the owners themselves used to leave their spades with her.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who exempted the gardener.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: Explains what Rav's ruling in this case did and did not mean.

terms.meaning: Someone who holds another person's property for safekeeping. Jewish law sets different levels of responsibility for a paid and an unpaid bailee if the item is lost or stolen.

bava_metzia-39b-3-5.note: An old woman with three daughters was taken captive together with one daughter. Of the other two, one died and left a young son. Abaye asked who should hold the old woman's property: not the surviving sister, since the old woman may be dead and the boy an heir; not the boy, since she may be alive. He ruled half to the sister and a steward for the other half; Rava said a steward for all of it. Later word came that the old woman had died. Abaye gave a third to the sister, a third to the boy, and split the captive daughter's third between the sister and a steward; Rava again said a steward for the whole of that third.
bava_metzia-39b-3-5.why: The Gemara has just ruled that a court never puts a relative in charge of a minor's property, lest he later be taken for its owner; this case works that rule out when the heirs are a child and a captive.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Works out how to divide the captive woman's property.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Holds that a steward should manage every uncertain share.

terms.meaning: A guardian appointed by the court to manage property for someone who cannot, such as a child or a captive.
A court letting a relative take over and work someone else's property while the owner is absent or too young.

bava_metzia-39b-6-9.note: A man from Bei Hozai came to the wealthy Mari bar Isak, said he was his brother, and demanded half the inheritance; Mari said he did not know him. Rav Hisda told the man to bring witnesses, but the man said they feared Mari, a violent man, so Rav Hisda made Mari prove the man was not his brother, over Mari's protest. Witnesses came and confirmed the brother, who then claimed half of the orchards Mari had planted as well, and Rav Hisda agreed, citing a mishna about older brothers who improve shared property. Rabba agreed, Abaye questioned it, and Rabbi Ami said Mari should be paid for his work. After messages went back and forth, Rabbi Ami learned the brother had been a minor and conceded that Rav Hisda was right.
bava_metzia-39b-6-9.why: The Gemara has just ruled that a court never lets a relative manage a minor's property; Rav Hisda's final answer rests on that rule, since Mari worked the land without court approval while his brother was a minor.

people.name: Mari bar Isak
people.about: A wealthy and violent man whose unknown brother claimed a share of the inheritance.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: The judge in the case.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: Agrees that the improvements are shared.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Questions whether the mishna fits Mari's case.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Argues Mari should be paid for his work, then concedes.

terms.meaning: A place far from where Mari lived, which is why the brothers did not know each other.

terms.term: the burden of proof rests upon the claimant
terms.meaning: The usual rule that whoever wants to take property from another must prove his claim.
Someone who works another's field for a share of the crop; here the measure for paying a relative who tended property.
The core collection of early rabbinic law; the Gemara is the later discussion built around it.

bava_metzia-42a-9-9.note: A man left money with another for safekeeping, and the keeper put it in a hut made of willow branches, from which it was stolen. Rav Yosef ruled the keeper liable: the hut was safe against thieves but careless against fire, so the loss began with negligence and ended by accident. Others report the ruling the other way, as exempt. The Gemara concludes that the keeper is liable.
bava_metzia-42a-9-9.why: The Gemara has been listing where money must be hidden to count as properly guarded; this case asks about a spot that is safe from one danger but not from another.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: The Sage who ruled on the stolen money.

terms.meaning: Someone who holds another person's property for safekeeping. Jewish law sets different levels of responsibility for a paid and an unpaid bailee if the item is lost or stolen.

terms.term: initially through negligence and ultimately by accident
terms.meaning: A loss where the keeper was careless, but the item was in the end lost in a way his carelessness did not cause.

bava_metzia-42a-10-10.note: A man left money with another for safekeeping. When he asked for it back, the keeper said he did not know where he had put it. The case came before Rava, who ruled that saying I do not know is itself negligence, and told the keeper to pay.
bava_metzia-42a-10-10.why: It is one of a run of cases on how a keeper must guard deposited money; this one sets the rule that a keeper who cannot say where he put it counts as negligent.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge who ordered the keeper to pay.

terms.meaning: Someone who holds another person's property for safekeeping. Jewish law sets different levels of responsibility for a paid and an unpaid bailee if the item is lost or stolen.
Careless guarding. A bailee who was negligent must pay for what was lost.

bava_metzia-42a-11-11.note: A man left money in another's care. The guardian gave it to his mother, who put it in a chest, and it was stolen. Rava asked how judges should rule. The guardian cannot simply be ordered to pay, because anyone who leaves something in another's care knows that his family may look after it. The mother cannot be ordered to pay, because her son never told her the money was not his, or she would have buried it. And the son can say that letting her think it was his made her even more careful. Rava ruled that the son swears he gave it to his mother, she swears she put it in the chest and it was stolen, and the son is exempt.
bava_metzia-42a-11-11.why: The Gemara is gathering rulings on when a guardian of money is negligent, such as hiding it in a willow hut or forgetting where it is; this case asks whether handing it to a family member counts.

people.name: Rava
people.about: He works through each party's defense and rules on the case.

terms.meaning: Someone who agrees to look after another person's property and may have to pay if it is lost through negligence.
A solemn sworn statement in court, used to settle claims that cannot otherwise be proven.

bava_metzia-42b-4-4.note: A guardian handling the affairs of orphans bought them an ox and handed it to a cowherd. The ox had no molars or teeth to eat with, and it died. Rami bar Hama asked how judges should rule. The guardian can say he gave it to the cowherd, and the cowherd can say he put it with the other oxen and threw it food, not knowing it did not eat. Since the orphans got their money back from the seller, the Gemara reasons, the claim comes from the seller, a trader who did not know of the defect: he swears he did not know, and the cowherd pays him the value of the meat at the cheapest price.
bava_metzia-42b-4-4.why: The Gemara is working through a run of cases in which property in someone's care passes through several hands and is lost, each asking how judges should rule; this one follows Rava's case of the guardian who gave money to his mother.

people.name: Rami bar Hama
people.about: The Sage who poses the question of how judges should rule.

terms.meaning: Someone paid to look after another's property; he must pay for losses caused by his lack of care.
A sale of an item with a hidden defect, which can be undone so the buyer gets his money back.
A person appointed to manage the property of orphans who are too young to manage it themselves.

bava_metzia-42b-9-9.note: A man left hops, used in making beer, in another's care. The guardian also had his own pile of hops, and he told his brewer to use hops from this pile, but the brewer went and used the other pile, the one left in his care. Rav Amram asked how judges should rule. The guardian can say he told the brewer which pile to use, and the brewer can say he was never told not to use the other one. The story itself does not give a ruling.
bava_metzia-42b-9-9.why: One of a run of cases in which property left in someone's care is lost through another person's hands; the discussion that follows asks whether the guardian is still to blame and what loss there really was.

people.name: Rav Amram
people.about: The Sage who poses the question of how judges should rule.

terms.meaning: A plant used in brewing beer.
Someone who agrees to look after another person's property and may have to pay if it is lost.

bava_metzia-44b-4-4.note: Rav borrowed gold dinars from the daughter of Rabbi Hiyya. By the time he came to repay, gold dinars had risen in value, and Rav worried that returning them would mean paying her interest. He went to Rabbi Hiyya, who told him: go and pay her back in good, full-weight dinars.
bava_metzia-44b-4-4.why: The Gemara is asking whether gold coins count as money or as goods compared with silver, and reads this ruling as showing Rabbi Hiyya treated gold as money. It then rejects the proof: Rav had dinars of his own elsewhere, which changes the case.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Founder of the academy at Sura in Babylonia; he had studied in the Land of Israel and was related to Rabbi Hiyya.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A leading Sage of the generation after the Mishna, Rav's teacher and uncle.

terms.meaning: The Torah forbids a Jew to pay or take any extra on a loan to another Jew, including repaying goods that have gone up in value.
A measure of volume for grain and produce. Lending a se'a of produce and getting a se'a back is forbidden, because prices may rise in between.

bava_metzia-46a-3-3.note: Rav Pappa had twelve thousand dinars owed to him in Bei Hozai. He transferred them to Rav Shmuel bar Aha by giving him the threshold of his house, so the coins passed to him along with the land. When Rav Shmuel bar Aha came back, Rav Pappa went out as far as Tevakh to meet him.
bava_metzia-46a-3-3.why: The Gemara has just concluded that coins cannot be acquired by a symbolic exchange; it notes that Rav Pappa, who had held they could, changed his mind, as shown by his using land to transfer these coins.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Owner of the money, who transferred it to Rav Shmuel bar Aḥa.

people.name: Rav Shmuel bar Aḥa
people.about: The man Rav Pappa sent to collect the money.

terms.meaning: A way of handing over movable things, such as coins, by attaching them to a transfer of a piece of land, here the threshold of a house.
A distant place where the money was owed.
A symbolic way of completing a deal, usually by handing over a cloth.

bava_metzia-48b-3-4.note: Buyers paid Rabbi Hiyya bar Yosef for salt. Then the price of salt rose, and he wanted to back out. He came to Rabbi Yohanan, who told him: go and give them the salt, and if not, accept upon yourself He Who exacted payment. The Gemara then retells the case: the money was only a down payment, Rabbi Hiyya bar Yosef thought it bought salt worth just that much, and Rabbi Yohanan told him it bought the whole order.
bava_metzia-48b-3-4.why: Abaye says one who reneges is only warned with He Who exacted payment; Rava says he is cursed and cites this case. The Gemara rejects the proof and recasts it as a case about down payments, opening the dispute that follows.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Cites the incident as proof for his view.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Yosef
people.about: A Sage who sold salt and wanted to back out when its price rose.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: The Sage he asked, who told him to deliver the salt.

terms.meaning: A formula from the mishna: the One who punished the generation of the flood and others will punish whoever does not keep his word. It is said to someone who backs out of a paid deal.
Part of the price paid up front to bind both sides to a deal.

bava_metzia-49a-3-3.note: Buyers paid Rav Kahana for linen. Then the price of linen rose. Rav Kahana came to Rav, who told him to give the buyers linen worth the money he had received; for the rest, his promise was only words, and going back on words alone is not bad faith.
bava_metzia-49a-3-3.why: The Gemara has been asking whether a down payment secures the whole deal or only its own worth; Rav's ruling follows the second view, and it introduces the dispute over whether breaking a spoken promise is bad faith.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A Sage who took money for linen and wanted to back out when the price rose.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who ruled on Rav Kahana's case.

terms.meaning: Breaking trust; going back on a commitment others relied on, which the Sages disapprove of even when the law cannot force it.

bava_metzia-49a-7-7.note: Rabbi Yohanan ben Matya told his son to go and hire workers. The son agreed to feed them, without saying what food. When he came back, his father told him that even a feast like King Solomon's would not fulfill the duty, since they are descendants of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Instead, before they began work, the son was to tell them they could claim only bread and legumes.
bava_metzia-49a-7-7.why: The Gemara is debating whether going back on a spoken promise is bad faith; it calls this an older dispute of the tanna'im, then asks how Rabbi Yohanan ben Matya could tell his son to change the terms.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Matya
people.about: The father, who sent his son to hire workers.

people.name: his son
people.about: Hired the workers and promised them meals.

terms.meaning: The Sages of the Mishna period, earlier than the Sages who debate in the Gemara.
The core collection of early rabbinic law; the Gemara is the later discussion built around it.

bava_metzia-49a-14-14.note: A man paid in advance for sesame. Then the price of sesame rose, and the sellers backed out: we have no sesame, take your money. He did not take it, and the money was stolen. Rava ruled that once they told him to take his money and he did not, the sellers were not even unpaid keepers of it. The Sages asked Rava whether the sellers still had to accept He Who exacted payment, and he said they did.
bava_metzia-49a-14-14.why: The Gemara has just argued that Rabbi Yohanan treats backing out of a spoken deal as bad faith; this case adds the risk for money a buyer leaves with sellers who back out.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge in the case.

terms.meaning: Two levels of keeper. A paid keeper must pay if the item is stolen; an unpaid one only if he was careless.
A formula from the mishna: the One who punished the generation of the flood and others will punish whoever does not keep his word. It is said to someone who backs out of a paid deal.

bava_metzia-49a-15-15.note: Rav Pappi reports from Ravina what Rav Tavot (some say Rav Shmuel bar Zutra), a man who would not bend the truth for the whole world, told him. One Friday at twilight a man stood at his door and asked if he had sesame to sell; he said no. The man asked to leave his dinars with him, since it had grown dark, and he answered: this house is before you. The man put the money in the house and it was stolen. Rava ruled that whoever says this house is before you is not even an unpaid keeper. Ravina asked about the Sages telling Rava that the seller must accept He Who exacted payment, and Rav Tavot said that never happened.
bava_metzia-49a-15-15.why: It follows the sesame case where Rava's ruling ended with the Sages demanding the curse; this eyewitness account places Rava's ruling in a different setting and denies the curse was ever raised.

people.name: Rav Pappi
people.about: Passes on the account he heard from Ravina.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Heard the account and asked about the Sages' remark.

people.name: Rav Tavot
people.about: A scholar famed for honesty who tells of what happened to him; some name him Rav Shmuel bar Zutra.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The judge in the case.

terms.meaning: Someone who keeps another's property as a favor; he must pay only if he was careless.
A formula from the mishna: the One who punished the generation of the flood and others will punish whoever does not keep his word. It is said to someone who backs out of a paid deal.
Friday at dusk, when the man could no longer carry money or get home before the Sabbath.

bava_metzia-49b-3-3.note: A man paid in advance for wine. Then he heard that men from the house of Parzak the vizier wanted to seize it. He told the seller: give me my money, I do not want the wine. The case came before Rav Hisda, who said that just as the Sages made pulling complete a sale for sellers, so they made it complete a sale for buyers.
bava_metzia-49b-3-3.why: The Gemara has been explaining why the Sages ruled that pulling the goods, not paying, completes a sale; Rav Hisda applies that rule to a buyer who wants out before taking the goods.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: The judge in the case.

people.name: Parzak
people.about: A vizier whose men wanted to seize the wine.

terms.meaning: Physically drawing goods into one's possession, the act the Sages made the step that completes a purchase of movable goods.

bava_metzia-51a-3-3.note: Rami bar Hama's landlord sold a donkey at a wrong price and was sad about it. Rami bar Hama asked why, heard what had happened, and told him to go and undo the sale. The landlord said too much time had passed, longer than it takes to show the goods to a merchant or a relative. Rami bar Hama sent him to Rav Nahman, who said that time limit applies only to a buyer; a seller may always back out.
bava_metzia-51a-3-3.why: The Gemara is discussing how long buyer and seller may undo a sale made at the wrong price, and why the merchants of Lod rejected Rabbi Tarfon's longer limit; this case sets the seller's rule.

people.name: Rami bar Ḥama
people.about: A Sage who noticed his landlord's distress.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: The Sage who ruled that a seller may always back out.

terms.term: time to show to a merchant or relative
terms.meaning: The mishna's limit for undoing a sale at an unfair price: only as long as it takes to show the goods to someone who knows the market.

bava_metzia-51a-5-5.note: A man was selling silk strips worth five ma'a. He asked six, though he would have taken five and a half. A buyer reasoned that if he bargained down to five and a half, he would count as having waived any claim, so he paid the full six, planning to sue for the overcharge. The case came before Rava, who ruled that the rule against overcharging covers only buying from a merchant; one who buys from an ordinary homeowner has no such claim.
bava_metzia-51a-5-5.why: This is the first of two matching cases that limit the overcharging rule to merchants. The Gemara next tells an identical case decided by Rav Hisda, then tests both rulings against the mishna, which says the rule applies to laymen as well.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage before whom the case came, and who ruled against the buyer.

terms.meaning: A small silver coin used in the prices here.
Selling something for more, or buying it for less, than its market value. Torah law forbids it, and the wronged party may reclaim the difference.

bava_metzia-51a-6-6.note: A man was selling jewelry worth fifty ma'a. He asked sixty, though he would have taken fifty-five. A buyer reasoned that if he paid fifty-five he would count as having waived any claim, so he paid the full sixty, planning to sue for the overcharge. The case came before Rav Hisda, who ruled that the rule against overcharging covers only buying from a merchant; one who buys from an ordinary homeowner has no such claim.
bava_metzia-51a-6-6.why: It repeats Rava's ruling in the silk case just before it. Rav Dimi and Rabbi Elazar then call the ruling correct, and the Gemara challenges it from a mishna that applies the overcharging rule to laymen; Rav Hisda answers that the mishna means goods made for sale.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The Sage before whom the case came, and who ruled against the buyer.

terms.meaning: A small silver coin used in the prices here.
Selling something for more, or buying it for less, than its market value. Torah law forbids it, and the wronged party may reclaim the difference.

bava_metzia-59b-1-10.note: Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis disputed whether a certain oven could become impure. Losing the argument, he called on a carob tree, a stream and the study hall walls to prove him right; each did, and the Rabbis rejected each. A Divine Voice declared that the law follows him, yet Rabbi Yehoshua answered, "It is not in heaven." Elijah later told Rabbi Natan that God smiled and said, "My children have triumphed over Me." The Sages burned what Rabbi Eliezer had declared pure and ostracized him. Rabbi Akiva, dressed in black, told him. He wept, crops were struck, and what he looked at burned. Rabban Gamliel nearly drowned until he prayed. Later his wife Imma Shalom, Rabban Gamliel's sister, found him praying face down and said, "You killed my brother"; just then a shofar announced his death.
bava_metzia-59b-1-10.why: The Gemara brings the story apropos of verbal mistreatment: it ends with Imma Shalom's teaching that the gates of prayer stay open for those who are wronged by words, and the discussion goes on to the verbal mistreatment of converts.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage who stands alone against the Rabbis on the oven and is ostracized.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: He rebukes the walls and rejects the Divine Voice, saying the Torah is not in heaven.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's disciple, who volunteers to tell him of his ostracism.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: The head of the Sages who ostracized Rabbi Eliezer; Imma Shalom's brother.

people.name: Imma Shalom
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's wife and Rabban Gamliel's sister, who guards her husband's prayers.

terms.meaning: A voice from Heaven that announces God's view; here the Sages refuse to decide law by it.
Placed under a ban: others must keep their distance, and the person behaves like a mourner.
The posture of a personal supplication prayer said after the main prayer; it is skipped on the New Moon.
A ram's horn; here it is sounded to announce a death.

bava_metzia-60a-10-10.note: Wine was brought to Rava from a store. He diluted it with water, tasted it, found it not tasty, and sent it back to the store. Abaye challenged him: the mishna says one may not sell such wine to a merchant even if he is told. Rava answered that his dilution was obvious to anyone, and that if one worried the storekeeper might add wine to sweeten it and resell it, there would be no end to the matter.
bava_metzia-60a-10-10.why: The mishna forbids selling wine mixed with water to a merchant even with a warning, since he may pass it on deceptively. This incident tests that rule against Rava's own practice and narrows it.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Sent diluted wine back to the store it came from.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Challenged Rava by quoting the mishna.

terms.meaning: The early code of Jewish law on which the Gemara comments; here, the passage on selling wine mixed with water.
Wine was normally drunk mixed with water; Rava mixed in water before drinking it.

bava_metzia-60b-4-5.note: An elderly slave dyed his hair and beard to look younger and asked Rava to buy him. Rava declined, citing the saying 'Let the poor be members of your household.' The slave then went to Rav Pappa bar Shmuel, who bought him. One day Rav Pappa asked him for water; the slave whitened his hair and beard and said, 'See, I am older than your father.' Rav Pappa applied to himself the verse 'The righteous is delivered from trouble, and another comes in his stead.'
bava_metzia-60b-4-5.why: The mishna forbids adorning a person, an animal or goods to make them look better before a sale. The Gemara asks what adorning a person means, and this slave's dyed hair is its example.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Declined to buy the slave.

people.name: Rav Pappa bar Shmuel
people.about: Bought the slave and found out he was older than he looked.

bava_metzia-63a-9-9.note: Rabbi Yehuda told the Sages of an incident: Baitos ben Zunin made a sale of his field on the instruction of Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, and the buyer ate the field's produce. The Sages answered that this proved nothing, since in that case it was the seller, not the buyer, who ate the produce.
bava_metzia-63a-9-9.why: A baraita rules that when a debtor sells his field to his creditor until the debt is paid, the creditor may not eat its produce, as that is like interest; Rabbi Yehuda permits it and cites this case as proof, which the Sages read the other way.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who permits the buyer to eat the produce, and tells this incident as proof.

people.name: Baitos ben Zunin
people.about: Made a sale of his field.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
people.about: Gave the instruction for the sale.

terms.meaning: The crops the field yields while the arrangement lasts.
A teaching of the early Sages that was left out of the mishna, the core code of Jewish law.

bava_metzia-64b-6-6.note: Rav Yosef bar Ḥama used to seize the slaves of people who owed him money and put them to work. His son Rava asked why. He cited Rav Naḥman: a slave is not worth even the bread he eats, so the owners lost nothing. Rava said Rav Naḥman meant idle slaves like his own slave Dari, who only dances among the wine barrels. His father then cited Rav: one who seizes another's slave and works him owes nothing, since the owner is glad the slave keeps working. Rava replied that this holds only when no money is owed; for a creditor it looks like interest. His father said: I retract.
bava_metzia-64b-6-6.why: The Gemara has just cited Rav Naḥman's ruling that a lender living in his borrower's courtyard must pay rent, so the stay does not look like interest. Rava uses that same ruling to show his father that working a debtor's slaves is the same problem.

people.name: Rav Yosef bar Ḥama
people.about: Rava's father, who seized the slaves of his debtors and made them work for him.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Rav Yosef bar Ḥama's son, who questions his father's practice and persuades him to stop.

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: Sage whose rulings both father and son cite.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Sage who ruled that one who seizes another's slave and works him is exempt.

people.name: Dari
people.about: Rav Naḥman's slave, who only dances among the wine barrels.

terms.meaning: Jewish law forbids a lender to take any benefit from a borrower beyond the loan itself; even a benefit that only looks like payment for the loan is forbidden.
Jewish law; the binding ruling on a question.

bava_metzia-66a-7-8.note: Rav Nahman decided a case in the Exilarch's court according to his own view, and Rav Yehuda tore up the resulting deed. The Exilarch told Rav Nahman, 'Rav Yehuda tore up your document.' Rav Nahman replied, 'Did a child tear it up? A great man tore it up; he must have seen a reason.' In another version he said, 'A child tore it up, for everyone is a child compared to me in monetary law.'
bava_metzia-66a-7-8.why: Rav Huna and Rav Nahman disagree over whether a lender who adds a forfeit-the-field condition after making the loan acquires the whole field. This is Rav Nahman acting on his view; right after it he retracts, persuaded that such a condition does not bind.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Decided the case in the Exilarch's court.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Tore up the deed Rav Nahman's ruling produced.

people.name: The Exilarch
people.about: In whose court Rav Nahman ruled; he reported the tearing to Rav Nahman.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, who kept his own court.
The written document giving the lender ownership of the field.

bava_metzia-66b-11-11.note: A man sold land with a guarantee to compensate the buyer if the seller's creditors ever took it. The buyer asked to be repaid, in that case, from the seller's very best land; the seller refused, wanting to keep it, but promised his other good land. In the end creditors seized the field, and a flood swept away the seller's very best land, leaving the other good land as his best. Rav Pappa thought the seller must still pay from the good land he had promised. Rav Aḥa of Difti asked Ravina why the seller could not say his promise assumed his best land would still exist, and that his good land had now taken its place. The text gives no final ruling.
bava_metzia-66b-11-11.why: Just before this, Rav Pappa ruled on land set aside to repay a debt. Here he again judges what a specific promise of land for repayment obligates, and his view is challenged.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Sage who thought the seller must keep his promise and pay from his good land.

people.name: Rav Aḥa of Difti
people.about: Sage who argued to Ravina that the seller could refuse.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Sage to whom Rav Aḥa of Difti put his argument.

terms.meaning: Jewish law grades land as best, middle and poorest. Normally a buyer whose land is seized is compensated from the seller's middle-quality land, so a promise of better land matters.
A seller's commitment to repay the buyer if the seller's creditors later seize the land he sold.

bava_metzia-67a-4-5.note: A woman asked a man to buy land for her from her relatives, and he did. The relative who sold it asked the agent, 'If I have money later, will you give it back to me?' The agent answered, 'You and she are relatives.' Rabba bar Rav Huna said that whenever the reply is 'you and she are relatives,' the seller is relying on working it out within the family, so he never fully resolved to transfer the land.
bava_metzia-67a-4-5.why: Because the sale was never final and the land goes back, the Gemara uses this case to ask whether the produce the buyer ate meanwhile counts as interest; Rabba bar Rav Huna and Rava rule it is only a 'hint of interest' that a court cannot take back.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage who ruled on what the agent's answer meant.

terms.meaning: Someone acting on another's behalf; here the man who bought the land for the woman.

bava_metzia-69a-6-7.note: Rav Elazar of Hagronya bought an animal and gave it to his sharecropper to fatten, paying him the head as wages plus half the profit. The sharecropper's wife told him that as a partner in the purchase he would get the tail too. So next time he bought an animal jointly with Rabbi Elazar, who gave him half the tail but then proposed splitting the head as well. When the sharecropper protested, Rabbi Elazar explained: before, the money was all his own, and without a little extra pay it would have looked like interest; now they were partners, and a sharecropper customarily works a little extra for the owner.
bava_metzia-69a-6-7.why: Rav and Shmuel have been debating how a man fattening another's calf must be paid so the deal is not interest, including Rav's idea of giving him the head. This case shows the extra payment is needed only when one side puts up all the money.

people.name: Rav Elazar of Hagronya
people.about: Bought an animal and gave it to his sharecropper to fatten; also called Rabbi Elazar.

terms.meaning: A worker who farms or tends someone else's property in return for a share of what it produces.
Payment for the use of money. Torah law forbids it between Jews, so any extra benefit to the one who supplied the money is suspect.

bava_metzia-69a-12-13.note: Two Samaritans ran a joint business. One divided their money without the other's knowledge, and Rav Pappa saw no loss, citing Rav Nahman: money counts as already divided. The next year they bought wine together, and the other partner divided it on his own; this time Rav Pappa asked him, 'Who divided it for you?' The man complained that Rav Pappa was pursuing him. Rav Pappa explained: when the money was split, nobody took the good coins and left the poor ones, but everyone knows some wine is sweet and some is not.
bava_metzia-69a-12-13.why: Abaye has just challenged a man who split animal offspring on his own, asking 'Who divided it for you?' These cases show when a partner may divide shared property alone; the Gemara then limits Rav Nahman's rule to coins of the same kind.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The judge who heard both cases.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The Sage Rav Pappa quoted: money counts as already divided.

terms.meaning: A community living in the Land of Israel that kept its own form of Israelite religion, apart from the Jews.

bava_metzia-69b-3-3.note: Rav Hama used to rent out dinars, charging a peshita a day for each one, reasoning that this was no different from renting out a hoe. All his money was lost. The Gemara explains his error: a hoe comes back itself and its wear is known, but coins do not come back as the same coins, and their wear cannot be known.
bava_metzia-69b-3-3.why: The Gemara is sorting out what counts as forbidden interest. This case draws the line between renting an object, which is allowed, and 'renting' money, which is really a loan with interest; Rava next allows paying a third party to arrange a loan.

people.name: Rav Hama
people.about: Rented out coins for a daily fee, and lost all his money.

terms.meaning: A silver coin.
A small coin; the translation gives it as one-eighth of a dinar.

bava_metzia-69b-5-5.note: Abba Mar, the son of Rav Pappa, used to accept pans of wax from wax makers and then ask his father to lend them money. The Sages complained to Rav Pappa that his son was taking interest. Rav Pappa replied that interest of this kind is fine: the Torah forbids only interest that passes from borrower to lender, and his son was simply being paid for putting in a word.
bava_metzia-69b-5-5.why: Rava has just ruled that a person may take a fee for asking someone else to make a loan; this case shows the ruling in practice.

people.name: Abba Mar
people.about: Son of Rav Pappa, who earned wax for arranging loans from his father.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage, head of an academy at Naresh.

terms.meaning: The Torah forbids a lender to take any extra from a Jewish borrower in return for a loan.

bava_metzia-70a-2-2.note: Rav Anan told Rav Nahman of a kettle that belonged to the children of Mar Ukva and was kept at Mar Shmuel's house. Mar Shmuel would weigh it before renting it out and weigh it again when it came back, and he charged both a rental fee and the value of the metal it had lost, although normally one charges one or the other, not both.
bava_metzia-70a-2-2.why: Rav Anan had quoted Shmuel as allowing interest on orphans' money, and Rav Nahman demanded the actual case. Rav Nahman answers that charging rent plus lost weight is allowed even for adults, since the owners bear the copper's wear.

people.name: Rav Anan
people.about: Reported Shmuel's ruling and told the incident.

people.name: Mar Shmuel
people.about: Kept the kettle and rented it out on behalf of Mar Ukva's children.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: Father of the children who owned the kettle; they were orphans.

terms.meaning: The loss of value as the copper kettle wore down with use, measured by weighing it.

bava_metzia-72a-8-9.note: A man mortgaged his orchard to another as security for a loan, and the lender ate its produce for three years. Then the lender threatened: sell me the orchard, or I will hide the mortgage document and say I bought it. The borrower went and transferred the orchard to his young son, and then sold it to the lender.
bava_metzia-72a-8-9.why: The Gemara rules this sale void, since the orchard was no longer the seller's, and asks whether the buyer can recover his payment from property the seller has since sold, as with a written loan. Abaye compares it to a ruling of Rabbi Asi and Rava rejects the comparison.

terms.meaning: Pledged as security for a loan; the lender held the orchard and ate its fruit until repaid.
After three years of use, a person holding land is presumed to own it, even without a deed. That is what makes the lender's threat work.

bava_metzia-73b-0-1.note: A gentile mortgaged a house to Rav Mari bar Rahel and then sold it to Rava. Rav Mari waited twelve months and then brought Rava rent, explaining that an unspecified mortgage runs a year, during which the gentile could not have removed him; from now on Rava should take rent. Rava replied that had he known the house was mortgaged to Rav Mari he would not have bought it. He would treat Rav Mari as the gentile's law would: as long as the loan was not repaid, no rent, and Rava would take none until he paid him off.
bava_metzia-73b-0-1.why: This sits in a run of cases where Sages' dealings are checked for hidden interest; Rava, just accused of taking interest himself, here refuses rent from a lender still living in the house on his loan.

people.name: Rav Mari bar Rahel
people.about: Lent money to a gentile and lived in the house the gentile mortgaged to him.

people.name: Rava
people.about: Bought the mortgaged house from the gentile.

terms.meaning: A non-Jew. The prohibition on interest does not bind a gentile, so a lender may live in his mortgaged house rent-free.
A mortgage with no term stated, which by default runs for one year.

bava_metzia-73b-4-5.note: Ravina used to pay the people of the fortress at Shanvata in advance for wine, and when they delivered it they poured him an extra jug. He asked Rav Ashi whether this was permitted. Rav Ashi said yes: they were simply forgoing it in his favor. Ravina objected that the land was not theirs. Rav Ashi answered that the land is pledged to the king for its tax, and the king says whoever pays the tax may eat the land's produce.
bava_metzia-73b-4-5.why: The Gemara is checking advance payments for wine for hidden interest, as in Rav Ashi's answer just before. The next case uses the same law of the kingdom for Sages who pay other people's taxes and then make them work.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Paid in advance for wine and was given an extra jug.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Ruled that the extra jug was permitted.

terms.meaning: The land tax owed to the king; whoever paid it had the right to the land's produce.

bava_metzia-75b-10-10.note: The Sages told Rav Ashi that Ravina keeps every directive of the Sages. Rav Ashi sent a messenger to him just before sunset on Friday asking for a loan of ten dinars to buy a small plot of land. Ravina replied that he should bring witnesses so they could write a document. Rav Ashi asked, 'Even me?' Ravina answered, 'All the more so you, who are busy with your studies and likely to forget, and I would bring a curse upon myself.'
bava_metzia-75b-10-10.why: Rav and Reish Lakish have just taught that lending without witnesses tempts the borrower and brings a curse on the lender. Ravina's answer puts that teaching into practice, and a baraita follows listing such a lender among those whose cries go unanswered.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Asked Ravina for a loan.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: Known for keeping every directive of the Sages; insisted on witnesses for the loan.

terms.meaning: Friday before sunset, the busiest time of the week as people prepare for the Sabbath.
A silver coin.

bava_metzia-78b-11-11.note: A man told others he had seen worm rot on the king's clothing. They asked him whether it was on the silver items or the gold ones. One version says he answered silver, and they killed him; another says he answered gold, and they let him be.
bava_metzia-78b-11-11.why: The mishna speaks of a rented donkey that became ill, and Rava explains the word as worm rot. This anecdote shows the same word in use.

terms.meaning: A disease caused by worms; in the Gemara's discussion, of a donkey's foot.
The translation explains these as linen and woolen garments. Worms are not found on linen, so the answer showed whether he was lying.

bava_metzia-81a-8-8.note: A man sold a donkey to another. The buyer said he would take it to a certain place: if it sold there, good; if not, he would bring it back. It did not sell, and on the way back the donkey was injured in an accident. The case came before Rav Nahman, who held the buyer liable.
bava_metzia-81a-8-8.why: A baraita just cited exempts a man returning unwanted goods if they break on the way back, as he is only like a paid guardian. Rabba objects with it, and Rav Nahman answers that this buyer would still have sold the donkey on his way back.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Judged the case and held the buyer liable.

terms.meaning: Legally required to pay for the loss.

bava_metzia-81a-13-14.note: A group of ice plant dealers took turns baking for one another, one each day. One day the others told one of them to go and bake for them, and he asked them to look after his cloak. Before he came back they were careless with it and it was stolen. Rav Pappa ruled that they had to pay for it. The Rabbis objected that this was negligence while the owner was working for them, and Rav Pappa was embarrassed. In the end it came out that at that very time the cloak's owner had been drinking beer, not baking.
bava_metzia-81a-13-14.why: The Gemara has just discussed the rule that a guardian who is in the owner's service, or has the owner in his, is exempt. This case tests that rule; right after it the Gemara asks why Rav Pappa was embarrassed and retells the case so that it fits both views of the law.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The Sage who heard the case and made the dealers pay for the stolen cloak.

terms.meaning: A group of traders in a particular plant who shared their baking, each taking a turn.
A case where a guardian is careless while the owner of the item is working for him. One view in the Gemara says the guardian is then exempt from paying.

bava_metzia-81b-0-0.note: A group of ice plant dealers took turns baking for one another. One day the others asked one of them to bake when it was not his turn, and he said: in payment for my baking, guard my cloak. Before he came back, the cloak was stolen. Rav Pappa ruled that they must pay for it. The Sages objected that this was guarding while the owner was working for them, which would excuse them, and Rav Pappa was embarrassed. Then it came out that at that time the cloak's owner had been drinking beer, not baking.
bava_metzia-81b-0-0.why: The discussion is about when guardians are excused because the owner was working for them. The Gemara retells this case to explain Rav Pappa's embarrassment even under the view that carelessness is never excused: baking out of turn made the dealers paid guardians.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: Judge who ruled the dealers liable for the stolen cloak.

terms.meaning: A rule that a guardian is not liable for loss if the owner of the item was working for him at the time.
Someone paid, in money or in kind, to guard another's property. A paid guardian must pay for theft or loss, unlike an unpaid one.

bava_metzia-81b-1-2.note: Two men were travelling, one tall and one short. The tall one rode a donkey and had a sheet; the short one walked, wrapped in a woolen cloak. At a river, the short man put his cloak on the donkey to keep it dry, took the tall man's sheet and covered himself with it, and the water washed the sheet away. The tall man came before Rava, who made the short man pay. The Rabbis objected that this was borrowing with the owner present, and Rava was embarrassed. In the end it came out that the short man had taken the sheet without the tall man knowing and put it back without his knowing.
bava_metzia-81b-1-2.why: It follows the case of Rav Pappa and the cloak, with the same shape: a ruling challenged on the rule that a borrower or guardian is exempt when the owner is with him, and then vindicated by a fact that came out later.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who made the short man pay for the lost sheet.

terms.meaning: When the owner of a borrowed item is with the borrower or working for him at the time, the borrower is not liable for loss. Taking without permission is not borrowing at all.

bava_metzia-81b-3-3.note: A man rented his donkey to another and told him: do not take the Nehar Pekod road, where there is water; take the Neresh road, where there is none. The renter took the Nehar Pekod road and the donkey died. When he came back he said: yes, I went by Nehar Pekod, but there was no water there.
bava_metzia-81b-3-3.why: Rava then rules the renter is believed, since he could have lied and said he took the other road; Abaye answers that this argument does not work where witnesses can be brought to show whether there was water.

terms.meaning: Two routes the owner names: the Nehar Pekod road has water along it, which he fears, and the Neresh road does not.

bava_metzia-83a-9-9.note: Some porters Rabba bar bar Hanan had hired broke a barrel of his wine, and he took their cloaks. They went and told Rav, who told him to give back their cloaks. Rabba bar bar Hanan asked whether that was the law, and Rav said yes, quoting Proverbs: "That you may walk in the way of good men." He returned the cloaks. The porters then said they were poor, had worked all day, were hungry and had nothing. Rav told him to pay their wages. Asked again if that was the law, Rav said yes: "And keep the paths of the righteous."
bava_metzia-83a-9-9.why: The Gemara has been discussing when carriers who break what they carry must pay, including Rav Hiyya bar Yosef's decree of half payment. Here Rav asks the employer to go beyond what the law strictly demands.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hanan
people.about: The employer whose wine barrel the porters broke, and who took their cloaks.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage the porters went to, who told Rabba bar bar Hanan to return their cloaks and pay them.

terms.meaning: Jewish law. Rabba bar bar Hanan asks whether Rav's instruction is what the law requires.

bava_metzia-83b-4-11.note: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, met an officer who arrested thieves and asked how he could tell them, since they hide like beasts; perhaps he took the righteous and left the wicked. The officer said it was the king's order. Rabbi Elazar taught him a test: a man dozing over his wine at the fourth hour who is not a scholar or a worker up early is a thief. The palace heard, and made Rabbi Elazar do the job himself. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha called him vinegar, son of wine. When a laundryman insulted him, Rabbi Elazar had him arrested; he later tried to ransom him and failed, and wept under the gallows. Told the man had sinned gravely, he rejoiced, yet was not at peace until his belly was cut open and the fat did not rot in the sun.
bava_metzia-83b-4-11.why: The Gemara has just read Psalms 104:20, "all the beasts of the forest creep forth," as the wicked of this world. The story opens with that verse and turns on rising early, a theme of the surrounding discussion about laborers' hours.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: A Sage who advised an officer how to catch thieves and was then made to arrest them himself.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha
people.about: A Sage who rebuked Rabbi Elazar for handing Jews over to be executed.

terms.meaning: An insult: a bad son of a good father, as vinegar is spoiled wine.
The hottest summer months in the Jewish calendar.
The Day of Atonement, the holiest day of the Jewish year.

bava_metzia-83b-13-13.note: Like Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, came to be arresting thieves for the government. Elijah the prophet met him and asked: until when will you hand over the people of our God to be executed? Rabbi Yishmael answered that it was the king's order. Elijah told him: your father fled to Asia; you flee to Laodicea. The text does not say what he did.
bava_metzia-83b-13-13.why: It comes straight after the story of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, as a matching case of a Sage serving the Roman authorities as a thief-catcher, this time rebuked by Elijah.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage who, like Rabbi Elazar, arrested thieves on the king's orders.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who rebuked Rabbi Yishmael and told him to flee.

terms.meaning: A city Elijah names as a place to flee to, as Rabbi Yishmael's father had fled to Asia.

bava_metzia-84a-2-3.note: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, were so fat that when they stood facing each other a pair of oxen could pass between them without touching them. A Roman noblewoman told them their children could not be theirs. They answered that their wives' bellies were bigger than theirs; she said that made it even less likely. Other versions give their answer as a verse, "For as the man is, so is his strength," or the saying "Love compresses the flesh."
bava_metzia-84a-2-3.why: Having told how both Sages served as thief-catchers, the Gemara turns to their bodies; afterward it asks why they answered so foolish a question at all, and says it was to protect their children's good name.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: One of the two very fat Sages.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: The other very fat Sage.

terms.meaning: A Roman noblewoman.

bava_metzia-84a-8-9.note: Rabbi Yohanan used to sit by the entrance to the ritual bath, saying that when Jewish women came up from immersing they should meet him, so they would have children as beautiful and as learned in Torah as he was. The Rabbis asked whether he was not afraid of the evil eye. He answered that he came from the descendants of Joseph, over whom the evil eye has no power, citing a verse about Joseph as read by Rabbi Abbahu.
bava_metzia-84a-8-9.why: The Gemara has been describing Rabbi Yohanan's beauty, and has just explained why he is missing from a list of beautiful men: he had no beard. This story continues that theme.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage famed for his beauty, who sat by the ritual bath so women would see him.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: A Sage whose reading of a verse about Joseph Rabbi Yohanan quotes.

people.name: Joseph
people.about: The biblical son of Jacob, from whom Rabbi Yohanan says he descends.

terms.meaning: A pool where a woman immerses after menstruation before she and her husband resume relations.
The belief that envious looks from others can cause harm.

bava_metzia-84a-11-17.note: Reish Lakish, a bandit, leapt into the Jordan after Rabbi Yohanan, who promised him his sister if he took up Torah. He did, and became a great scholar. Years later Rabbi Yohanan taunted him about knowing weapons as a bandit; hurt, Reish Lakish fell ill and died, and Rabbi Yohanan grieved until he lost his mind and died. The Gemara then returns to Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, who took suffering on himself, was blessed with wealth and ruled boldly, and asked to be laid in his attic when he died. His body stayed uncorrupted there for years, and a voice from the attic judged cases. When the Rabbis learned he was unburied, they brought him to his father's cave, where a serpent blocking the entrance opened to let the son in beside his father.
bava_metzia-84a-11-17.why: The Gemara has been discussing Rabbi Yohanan's beauty; the Jordan story begins there. It then picks up the unfinished story of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, to show that despite the proof of his righteousness he still did not trust himself.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage who drew Reish Lakish to Torah, gave him his sister, and grieved for him to death.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: A bandit leader who became a great scholar and Rabbi Yohanan's study partner; also called Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat
people.about: A Sage sent to comfort Rabbi Yohanan, who only agreed with him.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: A Sage who took suffering on himself; his body lay unburied in his attic for years.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: Rabbi Elazar's father, who in one version appeared in a dream asking for his son.

terms.term: under the wings of the Divine Presence
terms.meaning: Close to God; Rabbi Yohanan's way of saying he brought Reish Lakish into Jewish life and learning.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written code of Jewish law.
Here, ruling that a blood stain was not menstrual, so the woman was permitted to her husband.
The town where Rabbi Elazar's body lay, whose people did not want it moved.

bava_metzia-84b-13-18.note: As young men, Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi sat on the ground before the leading Sages, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa. Their sharp questions and answers led the Sages to give them benches. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi's father, protested that they were taking his only fledgling from him, so Rabbi was sent back to the floor; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa had Rabbi Elazar, who had no father to speak for him, sent back too. Rabbi Elazar was offended at being made Rabbi's equal, and from then on he knocked down Rabbi's arguments before he could make them. Rabbi complained to his father, who said: he is a lion son of a lion, and you are a lion son of a fox.
bava_metzia-84b-13-18.why: Rabbi Elazar's widow has just told Rabbi she did not know whether her husband was greater than him in Torah; the Gemara tells this to show that he was. It also explains why Rabbi named his father among three truly modest people.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Brilliant young scholar, raised to a bench and then sent back to the floor.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called Rabbi; son of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, seated with Rabbi Elazar as a young man.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: Leading Sage and Rabbi's father, who called himself a fox.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korḥa
people.about: Leading Sage who argued that Rabbi Elazar should be sent back to the floor too.

people.name: Jonathan, son of Saul
people.about: Named by Rabbi as modest, for telling David he would be second to him.

terms.meaning: Used alone, this title means Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
A family who led the Sages and, as the Gemara says, seated Hillel at their head and appointed him Nasi over themselves.
The title of the head of the Sages.

bava_metzia-85a-2-2.note: When Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) heard what Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, had gained through suffering, he said: afflictions are precious. He took thirteen years of afflictions upon himself: six years of kidney stones and seven of scurvy, or, some say, seven of kidney stones and six of scurvy.
bava_metzia-85a-2-2.why: Rabbi Elazar's widow told Rabbi that her husband was greater in deeds because he accepted afflictions. Here Rabbi responds by taking suffering on himself; the Gemara goes on to say his suffering was still not equal to Rabbi Elazar's.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who took years of suffering upon himself.

terms.meaning: Suffering that a person accepts on himself, believed to atone for sin and bring a person closer to God.

bava_metzia-85a-5-6.note: A calf being led to slaughter ran and hid its head in the corner of Rabbi's garment, weeping. He told it: go, this is what you were created for. In Heaven they said: since he had no compassion, let afflictions come upon him. Years later his maidservant was sweeping the house and sweeping out some young weasels. Rabbi told her to leave them, quoting "His mercies are over all His works." Heaven said: since he is compassionate, we will be compassionate to him, and his suffering ended.
bava_metzia-85a-5-6.why: The Gemara has just said that Rabbi Elazar's afflictions came and went out of love, while Rabbi's came and went because of incidents. This story tells those two incidents.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, whose suffering began and ended with how he treated animals.

bava_metzia-85a-8-11.note: Rabbi came to the town of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, and asked if that righteous man had a son. They said he did, and that any prostitute hired for two coins hired him for eight. Rabbi brought him back, ordained him and gave him to his uncle, Rabbi Shimon ben Isi ben Lakonya, to teach. Every day the young man said he was going back to his town, until his uncle shamed him and he vowed to stay. Grown into a scholar, he sat in Rabbi's academy, and Rabbi knew his father's voice in his. Rabbi applied to him and his uncle the verse "The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that is wise wins souls." When this Rabbi Yosei died, the serpent at his father's cave would not open for him, and people thought his father was greater.
bava_metzia-85a-8-11.why: It continues the account of Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon. The serpent echoes Rabbi Elazar's own burial, and the Divine Voice that follows says the son was not lesser, he had not suffered in the cave as his father had.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who rescued Rabbi Elazar's son and had him taught.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Rabbi Elazar's wayward son, who became a scholar.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Isi ben Lakonya
people.about: The young man's uncle, his mother's brother, who taught him Torah.

terms.meaning: Gave him the title Rabbi, here as a way to draw him into a life of learning.
A mark of the honor given to someone ordained as a Sage.

bava_metzia-85a-13-14.note: Rabbi came to the town of Rabbi Tarfon and asked whether that righteous man, who used to swear by the lives of his children, had a son. They said he had no son but had a grandson through his daughter, whom any prostitute hired for two coins hired for eight. They brought him to Rabbi, who said: if you repent, I will give you my daughter. He repented. Some say he married her and then divorced her; others say he never married her, so no one could say he repented for her sake.
bava_metzia-85a-13-14.why: It is told as a match to Rabbi rescuing Rabbi Elazar's son. The Gemara then asks why Rabbi took such trouble over wayward sons, and answers that whoever teaches Torah to another's son earns a seat in the heavenly academy.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who offered his daughter to bring the young man back.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: A righteous Sage who used to swear by the lives of his children; his daughter's son had gone astray.
